dailyBrief.text: Good morning, Smileys — it's homecoming day: Benji is expected to be discharged today, with his first pediatrician appointment already booked for tomorrow, and Solon is giving you a beautiful day for it, mostly sunny with a high near 73°. It is also Election Day: Ohio polls are open 6:30 AM to 7:30 PM, the governor's race between Amy Acton and Vivek Ramaswamy and the Senate race between Jon Husted and Sherrod Brown are both close, and 66 Cuyahoga County precincts — including some in Solon — have new polling places, so check yours before you go. Overnight the U.S. carried out limited strikes on Iranian missile targets on Qeshm Island while talks remained possible, and the Cavs lost a close one to Oklahoma City, 117-112, despite the game staying tight into the final minute. Tonight, after the ride home and a first evening as a family of four (plus Moose), the results start rolling in after Ohio polls close at 7:30.

Iran's leaders celebrate Trump's midterm loss and warn against new strikes
items.summary:
Iran's government said on Wednesday that American voters had rejected President Trump's war, even as Tehran stayed on high alert for renewed U.S. strikes. Parliament Speaker Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf, Iran's chief negotiator, posted that Americans had said no to war, and Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei warned in a written statement against any inclination toward submission to the United States.

The celebration was public and pointed. The newspaper Hamshahri put a blindfolded, bowed Trump on its front page under a headline about Iran's shadow over the elections, and the result landed on the anniversary of the 1979 seizure of the U.S. embassy in Tehran. Trump told Fox News the Iran war was part of the result, while also saying voters understood the importance of what he had done.

Behind the gloating, two senior Iranian sources told Reuters Tehran welcomed the Democratic victory but feared Trump might answer a political defeat with a military strike. Mediators have intensified efforts to end the war, Trump on Tuesday declined to rule out resuming combat, and Iran was planning wider retaliation if fighting resumes.

Senior Iranian officials told Reuters before the vote that Tehran had deliberately prolonged talks to weaken Trump politically. Watch whether that calculation now produces a deal — or a strike meant to prove the election changed nothing.

items.title: Russian bombing of a Ukrainian aid centre kills 40, with 59 people missing
items.summary:
The death toll from a Russian bombing of an aid distribution point in Komyshuvakha, in Ukraine's southeastern Zaporizhzhia region, rose to 40 by Wednesday, officials said — one of the deadliest strikes on civilians this year. A regional defence official wrote on Telegram that 59 people were still missing.

President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said Russian forces first dropped aerial bombs on an underground school building used as a distribution point as people arrived to collect aid, then struck the shelter again. The school handed out humanitarian aid every Monday and served as a shelter, about 11 miles from the nearest Russian positions. Two rescue workers and four police officers were among the dead, and Ukrainian police said the munitions included a 3-ton glide bomb.

Russia's Defence Ministry said the attack targeted Ukrainian military units around Komyshuvakha and two other settlements. Both sides deny deliberately targeting civilians.

The strike came days before the United States brings Ukrainian and Russian delegations together in Abu Dhabi on November 10-11 to discuss ending the war. A toll like this hardens Kyiv's hand — and tests whether Moscow arrives negotiating or escalating.

items.title: Russia hits power stations in Kyiv and Zhytomyr regions as temperatures fall
items.summary:
Russia hit two power stations in Ukraine's Kyiv and Zhytomyr regions on Wednesday, its defence ministry said, and also targeted a cargo vessel at sea near Odesa. The attacks followed Tuesday's missile and drone bombardments that knocked out power across swathes of the country.

Ukraine's emergency service and local officials said Poltava, Dnipro, Kirovohrad and Rivne regions were also hit. Ukraine's Energy Ministry said the week's strikes had forced nuclear plants to reduce output, emergency outages were cancelled in Kyiv on Wednesday but continued in Kharkiv, and rationing ran up to 16 hours a day in some regions. A drone attack near Krasnodar set fire to a logistics hub of the Russian retailer Ozon.

The pattern is deliberate: energy infrastructure, in waves, just as temperatures fall and a week before U.S.-brokered talks resume in Abu Dhabi. A Kremlin aide said last month that Moscow's attitude to three-way talks would depend in part on whether Ukraine launched a large-scale attack on Russia's National Unity Day, observed November 4.

Every plant knocked offline before winter is leverage at that table — and a repair bill Kyiv cannot easily pay while under fire.

items.title: Trump says the U.S. will stop $4 billion a year in aid to Israel after this year
items.summary:
President Trump said on Fox News that he and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had made a deal months ago to stop $4 billion in annual U.S. funding to Israel after this year, while still selling Israel weapons. He cast the move as removing a talking point he said left-wing Democrats used against Republicans.

The mechanics are unclear. The existing agreement provides $3.8 billion in U.S. military aid each year and does not expire until September 2028, and Trump did not explain how funding would be halted at year-end. Congress authorised the funding in a 2020 law, but the House and Senate must still pass appropriations bills each year to release the money — which now means a Democratic Congress holds that pen.

Neither the White House nor Netanyahu's office responded to requests for comment. Netanyahu's own position is uncertain after an October 27 election in which he lost his governing majority without opponents gaining a clear path to unseat him, and he had already said publicly that he expects U.S. aid to wind down over time.

A Quinnipiac poll in June found 48% of voters — and 66% of Democrats — believe the U.S. is too supportive of Israel. Watch whether the new Congress treats Trump's announcement as policy, or as an opening bid.

items.title: World leaders react to the Democrats' win: a 'new era,' warnings, and a wait-and-see from Moscow
items.summary:
Governments around the world spent Wednesday reading the same result and reaching very different conclusions. South African President Cyril Ramaphosa said the outcome would introduce a new era in world relations, Spain's Pedro Sánchez celebrated a vote against hatred and climate denial, and Norway's Jonas Gahr Støre called it a powerful signal of a change of course among American voters.

Moscow was cooler. Deputy Foreign Minister Sergei Ryabkov said the Democratic leadership's approach to Russia is sharply negative and nothing about that is new, while Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Trump remains in office and Moscow hopes he continues peacemaking efforts. Japan's Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara said the Japan-U.S. alliance remains the cornerstone of Japanese policy regardless of the outcome.

Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babiš predicted impeachment, vetoes and a kind of paralysis for the rest of Trump's term. Germany's AfD co-leader Alice Weidel said Trump's broken promise to avoid interventionist foreign policy had come back to haunt Republicans, and France's finance minister said Trump must acknowledge gasoline prices or scale back international involvement.

The through-line: allies and rivals alike now price in a Washington that cannot move fast — on Ukraine, trade, or Iran — for at least two years.

items.title: Spain's transport minister resigns after a train crash that killed 69
items.summary:
Spain's Transport Minister Óscar Puente resigned on Tuesday, six days after a high-speed train collision killed at least 69 people and injured dozens. The crash happened October 28 near Urda, about 130 km south of Madrid, when a Renfe train with 397 passengers ploughed into the back of a stationary Iryo train carrying 147.

Puente announced the decision in Congress after a lengthy session in which he outlined new rail safety measures and was grilled by the opposition. He said a transport minister in a country like Spain cannot remain in office after two accidents of this seriousness in less than a year.

It was Spain's second deadly rail accident this year and its worst crash since 2013; an earlier crash in January in Adamuz killed 46 people, for a combined toll of 115. On Wednesday Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez appointed Deputy Prime Minister Carlos Cuerpo to temporarily oversee the ministry, and the government announced a €30 million assistance package for victims' families.

Puente also withdrew as a candidate in the snap general election scheduled for November 29. The train drivers' union Semaf has announced strikes at Renfe for November 10 and 12 over working conditions and safety concerns.

items.title: Democrats take Congress and vow to rein in Trump as divided government looms
items.summary:
Democrats and Republicans squared up on Wednesday for what could be two years of deadlock, with Democrats vowing to use their midterm victory to rein in President Trump and Trump signalling he will keep flexing executive power. Democrats took the Senate with a majority of at least 54-44 and took the House, gaining at least 25 seats, with Senate races in Alaska and Mississippi still uncalled.

The scale was broad: Republicans lost ground in 99% of the roughly 2,100 counties where most votes had been counted by Wednesday morning. Democrats flipped more than two dozen House seats and won about a dozen races in districts Trump carried by double digits two years ago. House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries, on track to become the first Black Speaker, urged Trump to end the eight-month war on Iran before the new Congress is seated.

Trump posted an image of a red cap with the word VETO on it, congratulated Democrats for doing a good job in overnight interviews, and threatened to veto bills he called insane. Once seated in January, Democrats can investigate the administration and block Trump's nominees, including any Supreme Court vacancy.

First, though, the outgoing Republican Congress faces a must-pass bill to fund the federal government past December — the lame-duck session is where the new balance of power gets tested first.

items.title: Vance blames the Iran war entirely: 'The reason we lost is the war'
items.summary:
Vice President JD Vance distanced himself from President Trump's war on Iran on Wednesday, questioning its worth and blaming it entirely for the electoral rebuke that delivered Congress to the Democrats. 'The reason we lost is the war,' Vance wrote on X, adding that if anyone wanted to argue losing the Senate for the next six years was worth it, they should do so.

Vance said an earlier recommendation to end the war had been sound advice. He played down a split with the president, saying Trump also acknowledged the war cost Republicans — but Trump's own comments were far more measured, calling the war only a piece of the losses and telling the Wall Street Journal he did the right thing and would do it again.

An NBC News exit poll found 74% of voters said the Iran war was a crucial or major factor in their vote, and only 37% said the U.S. made the right decision to take military action. Vance listed voters' top priorities as ending the war, cost of living, putting America first, and changing the relationship with Israel.

Reuters noted the remarks could complicate Trump's deliberations on whether to restart major combat operations against Iran — a step officials say is still under consideration — and raise pressure on Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, whom some lawmakers are expected to try to impeach.

items.title: Speaker Johnson steps aside as Jordan and Scalise fight to lead House Republicans
items.summary:
House Speaker Mike Johnson told staff on Wednesday morning that he will not run for minority leader after Republicans lost control of Congress, according to sources familiar with the announcement. Johnson, who handily won re-election in his Louisiana district, is not expected to quit Congress.

Two contenders launched bids the same day: fellow Louisiana Rep. Steve Scalise, the current majority leader, and Ohio Rep. Jim Jordan, the House Judiciary Committee chairman. A person familiar with the situation said Johnson did not want to stand in the way of Scalise's ambitions. In a letter to House Republicans, Johnson said he would step away from leadership to spend more time with his wife Kelly and their four children.

Trump told reporters he would stay out of the race and said he did not ask Johnson to step down. House Republicans are scheduled to hold leadership elections next week, on November 10, by secret ballot.

Whoever wins leads a smaller, more Trump-sceptical minority into two years of divided government — while Hakeem Jeffries prepares to take the Speaker's gavel in January.

items.title: Democrats plan a long list of Trump investigations: 'Lawyer up'
items.summary:
With little prospect of passing major legislation while Trump holds the veto, the incoming Democratic majorities plan to use their other power: investigation. New House and Senate majorities give Democrats full investigatory authority, including subpoenaing records and compelling testimony.

Rep. Robert Garcia, expected to become House Oversight chair, put it in two words: 'LAWYER UP.' Democratic staffers named the administration's handling of and connections to Jeffrey Epstein as a primary target, alongside public corruption — alleged efforts by officials to advance the financial interests of the president, his family, themselves and close allies.

Other lanes include immigration enforcement, executive power, and the Iran war's authorisation — Congress's sole power to declare war and the requirement to seek approval for military force. Trump's personal projects are also flagged, from remodelling the White House East Wing and building a monumental arch to shuttering the Kennedy Center and paving the Rose Garden.

Rep. Jamie Raskin, the top Democrat on House Judiciary, is the other central figure. Expect the first subpoenas to land soon after the new Congress is seated in January.

items.title: Trump says 'I wasn't on the ballot' — and congratulates the Democrats who beat his candidates
items.summary:
President Trump watched the results from the White House and moved quickly to distance himself from them. 'I wasn't on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!' he posted on Truth Social, repeating the line to the New York Times, CBS News and Politico.

At the same time, he struck a cooperative note. 'My message is, congratulations to the Democrats, and I look forward to working with you for the good of our country,' he said, adding that he does not want to spend two years just vetoing everything — even as he posted a mockup of his signature red hat with VETO on the front. Asked by CBS if he was upset, he said he tried hard and left it on the field.

Trump told the New York Times he was absolutely willing to accept the results. He also singled out Texas Governor Greg Abbott, saying Abbott would not have lost had he not become a RINO in the last six months; Abbott lost to Democrat Gina Hinojosa.

Many of the losing candidates — in Texas, South Carolina, North Carolina and Georgia — were hand-picked by Trump. How much of the defeat he ultimately owns will shape the Republican fight over what comes next.

items.title: Dow jumps 1,569 points in its best post-midterm day in 44 years
items.summary:
U.S. stocks soared on Wednesday as Wall Street digested the Democratic sweep, reversing a sharp overnight slump in futures. The Dow closed up 1,569.40 points, or 3.03%, at 53,356.12 — its best day since April 2025 and its biggest post-midterm gain since 1982. The S&P 500 rose 1.58% to 7,688.62 and the Nasdaq Composite added 1.44% to 25,736.51.

The rally was led by the mega-caps and the economically sensitive names: Microsoft gained about 7%, Amazon about 6% and Apple about 5%, while hospital owners, dollar stores and solar stocks also jumped. Bond yields fell, the dollar weakened, gold rose more than 3% back above $4,000 an ounce, and the VIX volatility index sank almost 20% as investors welcomed certainty — and the prospect of gridlock curbing spending.

Not everything rose. AI infrastructure lagged on fears a Democratic Congress could restrict data centres: Nvidia fell about 3%, CoreWeave sank roughly 10%, and defence names dropped, with Lockheed Martin down about 7%. Oil fell sharply (see below), dragging energy shares with it.

Private payrolls rose 86,000 in October, beating forecasts, and services growth cooled only slightly with prices still high — a backdrop that keeps the Federal Reserve cautious even as politics hogs the tape.

items.title: AMD's data-centre sales nearly double to $8.55 billion, and it guides to about $17 billion next quarter
items.summary:
AMD beat expectations for its third quarter, reported Tuesday evening. Adjusted earnings were $2.09 a share, up 74% from a year earlier and ahead of the $1.95 consensus, on revenue of $13.38 billion, up about 45%.

The engine is the data centre. That segment's revenue reached $8.55 billion, up about 97% year over year — a record, and roughly 64% of total sales, up from about 47% a year ago — driven by demand for its EPYC server processors. Gross margin widened to 56%, and operating income rose about 75% to $3.92 billion. Client and gaming revenue fell 8% to $3.72 billion and missed expectations, with gaming down sharply.

For the fourth quarter AMD guided revenue to about $17 billion, above consensus, with data-centre sales expected to grow about 50% sequentially. Chief Executive Lisa Su said she expects overall revenue growth above 80% in 2027, with server revenue doubling.

Free cash flow fell to $554 million as the company builds for that demand. The question for investors is whether the AI build-out keeps absorbing supply at this pace — AMD's guidance says yes, for now.

items.title: Super Micro's sales nearly quadruple to $19.9 billion on AI server demand
items.summary:
Super Micro reported fiscal first-quarter net sales of $19.95 billion, up about 298% from a year earlier and 79% from the prior quarter, beating consensus of about $17.53 billion by roughly 14%. Adjusted earnings were $1.81 a share, well above both guidance and the $1.23 consensus.

AI solutions accounted for 71% of total revenue, up from 59% the prior quarter — a measure of how completely the company's fortunes now ride on AI data-centre build-outs. Gross margin improved to 12.8% on an adjusted basis, though it remains thin for the volumes involved.

Management raised full-year fiscal 2027 revenue guidance to $72-82 billion, from $65-72 billion, and guided the current quarter to $19.5-21.5 billion. Operations used $434 million in cash during the quarter as inventory and receivables grew with the ramp, and the results were labelled preliminary and unaudited.

Super Micro is the purest volume play on AI servers — which also makes it the most exposed if orders pause. Wednesday's guidance raise says its customers are not pausing yet.

items.title: Arm beats estimates on AI chip demand, but shares slip on a soft forecast
items.summary:
Arm reported fiscal second-quarter revenue of $1.44 billion on Wednesday, beating the $1.38 billion analyst average, with adjusted profit of 52 cents a share against 47 cents expected. Licensing revenue of $773 million comfortably beat estimates.

The soft spot was royalties: revenue there rose 8% to $670 million but missed the $720.8 million analysts expected. And the third-quarter forecast — $1.54 billion — was only marginally above the $1.53 billion consensus, disappointing investors who had priced in more. Shares fell about 3.5% in extended trading.

Chief Executive Rene Haas told Reuters there has been a huge pickup for all technology around the data-centre space. Arm says its server-chip architecture accounts for more than 50% of deployments at major cloud providers in 2025, heading above 60% by the end of 2026, and it now expects $2 billion of AGI CPU sales across fiscal 2027 and 2028 from the complete-chip business it launched in March.

A Delaware jury last month found Arm breached parts of its Qualcomm licensing agreement but awarded only $2 in damages, leaving royalty disputes to a judge — a reminder that Arm's licensing model is both its strength and its legal exposure.

items.title: Qualcomm beats estimates as car chip sales jump 89%, but shares slip after hours
items.summary:
Qualcomm reported fiscal fourth-quarter results after Wednesday's close that just topped expectations: adjusted earnings of $2.17 a share against a $2.16 consensus, on revenue of about $10.4 billion.

The standout was automotive. Car chip revenue surged 89% year over year to $1.99 billion, comfortably ahead of expectations, continuing a run that saw the segment set records in prior quarters. Handset chip sales of $5.14 billion came in below Wall Street expectations, and data-centre-related revenue was about $650 million as the company pushes into a market dominated by others.

Despite the beat, shares came under pressure in after-hours trading on muted guidance: Qualcomm guided the current quarter to earnings of $2.15-2.35 a share on revenue of at least $10.4 billion, against consensus looking for more.

The mix tells the strategy: phones are mature, cars and data centres are the growth story. An 89% jump in automotive only matters if it holds as carmakers' own demand cycles turn.

items.title: Oil plunges nearly 9% as traders bet the Iran war may wind down
items.summary:
Oil crashed on Wednesday as the midterm result — and the Republican blame game that followed — convinced traders the Iran war may wind down. Brent settled down about $9.27, or 8.9%, at $94.29 a barrel, its lowest since early September, after trading near $118 on Friday. U.S. crude fell about 8.3% to $88.08.

The triggers were political. Trump told Fox News on election night that he thought gasoline prices explained the Republican defeat, and Vice President Vance posted that the war was the reason for the losses. Trump had also told the Financial Times that Washington had no immediate plans to strike Iran, and a Qatari outlet again reported significant progress in U.S.-Iran negotiations — claims a senior Iranian official had swiftly dismissed the day before.

Brent is down about 20% on the week, on course for its biggest weekly fall since April 2020. U.S. crude inventories fell about 900,000 barrels to 409.8 million in the week ended October 30, roughly 4% below the five-year average.

One caution from traders: Rapidan Energy's Bob McNally warned that bets on the administration quitting the war may be premature, arguing escalation remains possible. Oil has priced in peace quickly before — and been wrong.

items.title: Florida rivers keep rising, with major flooding forecast into the weekend
items.summary:
Florida's flooding is not over — it is moving into the rivers. On Wednesday morning the National Weather Service in Melbourne raised the forecast for the St. Johns River near Cocoa to major flooding: the river stood at 16.7 feet, above its 16.0-foot flood stage, and was expected to reach major stage late this week and stay there into the weekend.

At 17 feet, water approaches low-lying homes in the Silver Pines subdivision and in Rockledge and Cocoa. Above Lake Harney in Seminole County the river was at 8.5 feet and forecast to rise to 9.8 feet by Monday, with low homes flooding and many secondary roads impassable at 10 feet. Near Sanford, minor flooding was expected Thursday and rising.

On the Gulf side, the Peace River at Arcadia was forecast to crest at 16.5 feet Thursday evening — above the 16.0-foot record crest from February 1998 — with up to 60 homes at River Acres at risk at that level.

River flooding lags the rain by days, which is why a storm that has passed can still be rising. Anyone near these rivers should treat the weekend forecasts as the event, not the aftermath.

items.title: Southwest floodwaters recede, leaving a sea of mud, shattered homes and weeks of cleanup
items.summary:
Skies began clearing Tuesday across the Southwest, but floodwaters from almost two weeks of on-and-off heavy rain still inundated some areas while others began digging out of the mud. More than 20 trillion gallons of rain fell on the Four Corners states and Nevada in two weeks — about 10 months of flow over Niagara Falls.

In Pagosa Springs, Colorado, downtown remained closed to traffic Tuesday as heavy equipment cleared mud, water and debris; walkways and bridges collapsed or were heavily damaged, and cleanup could take weeks or more. The San Juan River at Shiprock, in the Navajo Nation, crested at 19.8 feet early Tuesday before falling. One person died in the floodwaters, and police suspect a second death was weather-related.

Colorado Governor Jared Polis declared a disaster emergency for 12 southwest counties, about 100 National Guard members were mobilised, and a disaster assistance centre was set to open Thursday in Pagosa Springs. In Durango, one resident described nearly five feet of water entering her home, surrounded by about two feet of mud.

The same system soaked Florida, where more than 20 polling places had to be changed after an emergency declaration. Recovery in both regions is measured in weeks, not days.

items.title: A Washington resident is the first U.S. bird flu death of 2026
items.summary:
A Yakima County, Washington resident died on Sunday, November 1 after contracting H5N1 bird flu through exposure to infected dairy cattle — the first human bird flu death in the United States in 2026, and the third since 2024. Genetic sequencing confirmed the virus was the B3.13 strain circulating in U.S. dairy herds since 2024, matched to samples from two Yakima County farms.

It was the third human infection in Yakima County since mid-October, all linked to dairies with infected cows. Washington's first cattle detections came on October 8, and state trackers listed about 40 infected herds in Yakima and Benton counties by the end of October — the first bird flu ever found in Washington cattle.

Health officials stressed the risk to the general public remains low. There is no evidence the virus has adapted to spread more easily between people, and no human-to-human transmission has been documented in the U.S. The county health district and state health department are identifying and monitoring close contacts.

Before this case, the CDC counted 72 confirmed human H5N1 cases and two deaths in the U.S. since 2024. The death is a reminder the dairy outbreak is still expanding into new states even as human cases stay rare.

items.title: Voters reject AI data centres in almost every local ballot measure — and Ohio led the revolt
items.summary:
Voters across the country used Tuesday's ballots to say no to AI data centres. More than 40 measures were decided across 10 states, and opponents were successful in virtually all of them — by one count, the industry prevailed in just a single community.

Ohio had the most measures of any state — 21 across roughly 18-20 jurisdictions — and every jurisdiction with reported results voted against development. In Ashville, voters repealed the EdgeConneX agreement by 1,468 to 330, covering two buildings and an on-site gas plant on about 195 acres where construction was already under way. Wilmington rejected four rezoning proposals by about 80% to 20%. Elsewhere, El Dorado, Kansas approved a 10-year ban on high-impact data centres by 71% to 29%.

The only industry win came in Harwood, North Dakota, where voters rejected a charter amendment that would have required independent review of large industrial projects. An August poll found 75% of registered voters opposed a new data centre near their home, and an NBC exit poll found 56% of midterm voters called AI and data centres a crucial or major factor, with most of those voting Democratic.

Some of these votes are advisory rather than binding. But developers now face a map where local consent — not just power and land — is the scarce resource.

items.title: Florida's Treasure Coast roads stay impassable as shelters move and evacuations continue
items.summary:
Major roadways across Florida's Treasure Coast remained impassable on Wednesday after historic rainfall, law enforcement said, with closures in Martin and St. Lucie counties including stretches near the Savannas Preserve and the North Fork of the St. Lucie River. Port St. Lucie police were evacuating residents in the Vitalia at Tradition community affected by flooding.

Shelters were relocated Wednesday so schools could reopen: the general population shelter moved to the Havert L. Fenn Center in Fort Pierce, and the special medical needs shelter moved to the health department facility in St. Lucie. As of 9 a.m., 16 people were in the general shelter and five in the medical needs shelter.

A National Weather Service meteorologist called November 2 at least a 500- to 1,000-year rainfall event, with about 12 inches near I-95 in Port St. Lucie. Wider reporting put 24 inches in 36 hours on Malabar in Brevard County, called it Melbourne's wettest day in 89 years, and counted two deaths and hundreds of rescues across the region.

Officials warned the water may take several days to recede: water control structures are open, but King Tides left the floodwater nowhere to flow.

items.title: Amy Acton wins the Ohio governor's race — the first woman elected to the job — and Ramaswamy concedes
items.summary:
Democrat Amy Acton defeated Trump-backed Republican Vivek Ramaswamy to become the first woman elected governor in Ohio history, and the first Democrat to win the office in 20 years. Acton, the former Ohio Department of Health director and a first-time candidate, led 52.31% to 44.38% in one statewide summary, with the Associated Press showing 98% of precincts reporting — comfortably above Ohio's automatic recount threshold.

Ramaswamy conceded on Tuesday night, saying Ohioans were rooting for the success of her administration, and said he had called Acton and left a message congratulating her. Acton said Ohio had chosen unity and decency and promised to work with anyone to make life better in the state.

She campaigned on high costs, property and income tax relief, public education and tougher requirements for data centres. The race was not without a flashpoint: Ramaswamy aired an ad featuring Acton's estranged mother accusing her of lying, which his campaign said carried $4 million in airtime.

Acton takes office in January facing a Republican Ohio Senate that kept its supermajority — and a House that just lost its one (see below). How she governs across that split is the story of 2027.

items.title: Sherrod Brown wins back a U.S. Senate seat, beating Jon Husted in the special election
items.summary:
Former Senator Sherrod Brown completed his comeback on Tuesday, defeating incumbent Senator Jon Husted in the special election to fill the seat JD Vance won in 2022 before becoming vice president. The term runs to January 2029. Brown led 50.01% to 45.15% in a statewide summary, with the AP showing 98% of precincts reporting.

Brown lost re-election in 2024 after roughly 30 years in Congress; two years later he is going back, and his win helped Democrats retake the Senate majority. In his victory remarks he promised fights to end the tariffs, end the war, lower costs and raise paychecks.

The campaign turned on economic anxiety: Brown hammered Husted over data centres and rising utility costs, and voters cited higher grocery, gas, health insurance and electricity prices. Husted aligned closely with Trump and appeared with him at three late rallies. The race drew more than $500 million in political advertising this cycle.

Brown returns as one of the Senate's most senior economic populists — in a majority that will need his vote on everything from nominees to war powers.

items.title: Ohio Democrats win 8 of 15 U.S. House seats as Miller, Turner and Carey all lose
items.summary:
Ohio Democrats will hold 8 of the state's 15 U.S. House seats, up from five, after defeating three Republican incumbents on Tuesday. In the Cleveland-area 7th District, union ironworker Brian Poindexter beat Rep. Max Miller with about 54-55% of the vote; Miller conceded in a post on X. Poindexter carried Cuyahoga County with 61%.

In the Dayton-area 10th, Kristina Knickerbocker defeated Rep. Mike Turner, a former mayor who had served in Congress 23 years, by about 49% to 47% with all precincts reporting unofficially. In the Columbus-area 15th, former Ohio State professor Don Leonard upset Rep. Mike Carey by about 52% to 45%.

Democratic incumbents held the rest: Marcy Kaptur, the longest-serving woman in Congress, beat Derek Merrin 53-47 in the 9th; Emilia Sykes won the 13th; and Greg Landsman, Joyce Beatty and Shontel Brown also won.

Miller's campaign had been overshadowed by domestic violence allegations from his ex-wife, which he denies. All results are unofficial until certified, but none of the three flips is within recount range on current numbers.

items.title: Democrats sweep Ohio's statewide offices for the first time since 2008, as the last Republicans concede
items.summary:
The concessions landed through Wednesday and completed a sweep two decades in the making. Attorney General Keith Faber conceded early Wednesday to John Kulewicz, a first-time statewide candidate who becomes the first Democratic attorney general since Richard Cordray in 2008; the margin was about 50.31% to 49.69%. Jay Edwards conceded the treasurer's race Wednesday to Cincinnati council member Seth Walsh, who led by roughly 50,000 votes.

Allison Russo won secretary of state — Ohio's chief elections officer — with Robert Sprague conceding before 11 p.m. Tuesday; Russo is the first Democrat to win a down-ballot statewide office since 2008. Republicans held one executive office: Frank LaRose, the current secretary of state, won auditor over Maple Heights Mayor Annette Blackwell, about 50.79% to 49.21%.

On the Ohio Supreme Court, Democrats held Justice Jennifer Brunner's seat and flipped another, with Marilyn Zayas beating incumbent Justice Dan Hawkins by about two points; Zayas would be the first Latina on the court. Democrats now hold two of seven seats.

All of these margins sit above Ohio's 0.25% statewide automatic recount threshold. Secretary of State Russo also sits on the Ohio Redistricting Commission — a seat with long consequences beyond this cycle.

items.title: 'Cheaters': the Clase and Ortiz pitch-rigging trial opens in Brooklyn
items.summary:
Opening statements in the pitch-fixing trial of Cleveland Guardians pitchers Emmanuel Clase and Luis Ortiz were delivered Wednesday in Brooklyn federal court, after a two-day jury selection. Assistant U.S. Attorney Rebecca Urquiola told the jury the defendants are cheaters who sold their pitches.

Prosecutors say Clase befriended a gambler in the Dominican Republic in early 2023 and agreed to tip what pitches he would throw, enabling gamblers to win at least $460,000 on ball-and-strike prop bets. Clase is accused of rigging at least 18 pitches across 17 games from May 2023 to May 2025, sometimes using the code words 'chicken' or 'rooster' in texts, and of recruiting Ortiz in 2025. Ortiz is accused over two pitches in June 2025. Both have pleaded not guilty and face up to 65 years if convicted on all counts.

The defences diverged. Clase's lawyer said gambler Enoc Pena falsely claimed to have inside information and was selling lies — fellow gamblers lost more than 200 bets on Clase pitches. Ortiz's lawyer said Ortiz had no contact with gamblers and that two balls are not a conspiracy, just baseball.

The trial is expected to last about three weeks, with possible witnesses including pitching coach Carl Willis, several catchers and general manager Mike Chernoff. It is the first of five recent federal sports-gambling cases to reach trial.

items.title: Democrats break the GOP supermajority in the Ohio House, with four races headed toward recounts
items.summary:
Democrats declared victory in eight Ohio House seats previously held by Republicans, dropping the GOP below the 60-seat supermajority it had held since 2013. If current leads hold, the House would sit at 56 Republicans to 43 Democrats — meaning Governor-elect Acton will not face a veto-proof House, though the Ohio Senate kept its Republican supermajority after losing only two seats.

The flips included Megan Coy beating Rep. Mike Dovilla of Berea, Rose Lounsbury unseating Rep. Andrea White of Kettering, Krista Allison unseating Rep. Jim Thomas, and Shelby Kimball unseating Rep. Brian Lorenz, plus four open-seat wins.

Four more races are too close to call: Rep. Cindy Abrams leads by just 19 votes, Tom Herner leads Rep. Tom Young by 134, Haraz Ghanbari leads by 126, and Edward Schimmel holds a slim lead. District races trigger an automatic recount below 0.5%, and county boards must complete their canvass by November 24.

Analysts expect a lame-duck push in Columbus before Acton takes office in January, while both parties watch those four recounts — each one changes how much room she has to govern.

baby.tip: Homecoming day tip: before you leave the hospital, do the car-seat check while help is still right there — base tight, straps snug at armpit level, and Benji's first ride home in a rear-facing seat in the back. Then tonight, keep it simple: one bag unpacked, feeding log started, and the diaper bag restocked for tomorrow's first pediatrician visit. If anything about feeding, breathing or temperature worries you at home, call the pediatrician or your OB team — that's exactly what they're there for.
baby.fact: Newborns sleep a lot but in short stretches — typically 16 to 17 hours a day, broken into naps of just a few hours at a time, because their tiny stomachs need frequent feeding. Benji's sleep will feel random this first week; short, frequent stretches around the clock are completely normal for a brand-new baby.
baby.fun: Today's tiny mission: the first family photo at home — Mike, Kelly, Benji and Moose in one frame (Moose at a calm, supervised distance for take one). It doesn't need to be perfect; the slightly chaotic version is the one you'll love most in a year.
